case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ERISA imprudent-investment claim based on underperformance plausibly pleads a breach of the duty of prudence without alleging a “meaningful benchmark” for comparison.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA § 404(a)(1) (29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1))—duty of prudence (and related fiduciary duties); also implicated in parts of the record: ERISA § 104(b)(4) (29 U.S.C. § 1024(b)(4)) for document-disclosure claims; Article III standing principles (U.S. Const. art. III) discussed in relation to informational/procedural injury.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners contend that for claims predicated on fund underperformance, it should be enough at the pleading stage to allege that fiduciaries failed to act with ERISA-required “care, skill, prudence, or diligence” under the circumstances, without having to identify and plead a specific “meaningful benchmark” (such as a particular index or peer group) to make the claim plausible. They seek Supreme Court review to resolve/clarify the pleading standard for indirect imprudence allegations where plaintiffs infer imprudence from alleged underperformance.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the Ninth Circuit correctly affirmed dismissal because plaintiffs’ allegations were internally inconsistent (criticizing risk/alternatives while also claiming a conservative strategy lost returns), overly generalized (attacking hedge funds/private equity in the abstract), and failed to provide the necessary comparative context to infer imprudence—i.e., a “sound basis for comparison” or meaningful benchmark. They further argue certiorari is unwarranted because the case is factbound and a poor vehicle: the plans used a post-2008 risk-mitigation strategy with diversified alternative investments typical in large institutional portfolios, making it atypical for resolving a general pleading rule. They also suggest that if the Court were to take up the benchmark issue, this case is a better vehicle than Parker-Hannifin due to Parker-Hannifin’s interlocutory posture and an apparent Justice recusal risk there, but maintain neither case merits review.
key_precedents: Va. Mil. Inst. v. United States, 508 U.S. 946 (1993)
Meiners v. Wells Fargo & Co., 898 F.3d 820 (8th Cir. 2018)
Thole v. U.S. Bank N.A., 140 S. Ct. 1615 (2020)
Magadia v. Wal-Mart Associates, Inc., 999 F.3d 668 (9th Cir. 2021)
Strubel v. Comenity Bank, 842 F.3d 181 (2d Cir. 2016)
Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 541 U.S. 913 (2004)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry point has force: a rigid, index-by-name “benchmark” prerequisite could screen out meritorious ERISA claims before participants can access comparative data. But as Justice Kagan explains, § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” language makes prudence inherently comparative, so when plaintiffs use underperformance as the proxy for imprudence Rule 8 plausibility ordinarily requires some coherent comparative context—without converting that into a categorical element barred by Hughes. Dudenhoeffer’s instruction for careful, context-sensitive pleading scrutiny supports this narrower approach: it screens out hindsight-based outcome pleading while leaving room for alternative factual allegations (fees, objectives, process failures) to supply the needed context. On this record, the Ninth Circuit’s “sound basis for comparison” analysis is best read as that context-sensitive plausibility screen, so I would affirm on narrow grounds without announcing a bright-line benchmark rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress the information asymmetry at the pleading stage, but that policy concern cannot override what ERISA’s text and Rule 8 require: § 1104(a)(1)(B) asks what a prudent fiduciary would do “acting in a like capacity” and “under the circumstances then prevailing,” which makes the inquiry inherently comparative. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, affirmance need not adopt a categorical index-by-name requirement, but when underperformance is offered as the proxy for an imprudent process, plaintiffs must plead some coherent comparative context so the inference of imprudence is plausible rather than hindsight. Hughes’s rejection of per se rules does not eliminate Twombly/Iqbal and Dudenhoeffer’s directive for context-sensitive screening of conclusory outcome-based allegations; it instead confirms we should avoid bright lines while still demanding nonconclusory facts. On this record, the Ninth Circuit’s “sound basis for comparison” is best understood as that textual and procedural plausibility requirement, not an extra-statutory element.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize the information asymmetry at the pleading stage, and we should not create a categorical “benchmark-by-name” prerequisite that would function as an extra-textual element. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, § 1104(a)(1)(B) is inherently comparative (“like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing”), and under Dudenhoeffer plus Twombly/Iqbal, a complaint that uses underperformance as the proxy for imprudence must allege some coherent comparative context (not necessarily an index) to make the inference plausible rather than hindsight. Hughes’s rejection of bright-line rules supports that narrow, context-sensitive approach; it does not authorize conclusory “we would have done better” allegations to unlock burdensome discovery untethered to what a prudent fiduciary would have done at the time. On this record, I agree with Justice Roberts that the Ninth Circuit’s “sound basis for comparison” functions as a plausibility screen, and the pleaded comparisons are too mismatched and internally inconsistent to state a claim.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach seriously: when a theory rests primarily on underperformance, some comparative context is often needed to make the inference of imprudence plausible. But I remain concerned that the Ninth Circuit’s “sound basis for comparison” formulation, as applied, risks hardening into an implicit pleading element that effectively demands a like-for-like comparator before any discovery, notwithstanding Hughes’s warning against such gatekeeping rules. Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” should screen out pure hindsight, yet it should also recognize that plaintiffs can plausibly allege imprudence through concrete context other than a named benchmark—fees, strategy/objectives, and persistent deviation from stated aims—especially where fiduciaries control the most informative comparative data. Justice Kagan is right that prudence is comparative, but comparability can be plausibly alleged without turning “benchmark” into a near-dispositive pleading hurdle that undermines access to justice for plan participants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry point is the hardest: if we effectively require a named “meaningful benchmark,” many plausible ERISA claims could be screened out before participants can access comparative data. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s narrower approach that we can avoid any categorical benchmark element while still applying Rule 8 plausibility in a way that respects § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s inherently comparative text (“like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing”): when underperformance is the principal proxy for imprudence, the complaint ordinarily must supply some coherent comparative context (not necessarily an index) to distinguish bad outcomes from an imprudent process. Dudenhoeffer’s insistence on “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage reinforces that courts should not infer breach from hindsight results alone, and Hughes’s anti-bright-line instruction is satisfied so long as we make clear that other concrete allegations (fees, objectives, process failures) can also plausibly plead imprudence. On this record, as Justice Barrett notes, the pleaded comparisons are mismatched and internally inconsistent, so the Ninth Circuit’s “sound basis for comparison” operates as a contextual plausibility screen rather than an extra statutory element.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern is real, but it cannot justify letting a complaint proceed on bare underperformance labels untethered to any like-for-like context; § 1104(a)(1)(B) asks what a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would do “under the circumstances then prevailing,” which is inherently comparative. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, affirmance need not adopt a categorical “benchmark-by-name” element forbidden by Hughes; it can rest on ordinary Rule 8 plausibility, requiring enough coherent comparative facts (in whatever form) to make “underperformance” meaningful rather than hindsight. Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage reinforces that courts must screen out conclusory outcome-driven claims where the alleged comparators are mismatched or internally inconsistent. On this record, the Ninth Circuit’s “sound basis for comparison” framing functions as that plausibility check, not as an extra-textual pleading hurdle.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to flag information asymmetry and the risk that a “meaningful benchmark” demand hardens into an extra element at Rule 12, but that concern is answered if we frame the requirement as Chief Justice Roberts does: not an index-by-name rule, but Rule 8 plausibility applied to ERISA’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” language. Where, as here, underperformance is doing essentially all the work as a proxy for an imprudent process, Dudenhoeffer’s context-sensitive scrutiny and Twombly/Iqbal require some nonconclusory comparative context—Justice Kagan’s “sound basis for comparison”—to avoid inferring breach from results and inviting hindsight litigation. Hughes cautions against categorical pleading rules, yet it does not relieve plaintiffs of alleging facts that make the prudence inference plausible; on this record, the Ninth Circuit permissibly found the pleaded comparisons mismatched and internally inconsistent given the post-2008 risk-mitigation strategy. I therefore would affirm on narrow grounds, emphasizing alternative ways plaintiffs can plead imprudence (fees, objectives, process failures) when available, but holding this complaint insufficient as pled.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry point has force, but it cannot displace Rule 8’s requirement that a complaint supply nonconclusory facts making breach plausible rather than inferable from results alone. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s text is inherently comparative (“like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing”), so when underperformance is the asserted proxy for an imprudent process, plaintiffs ordinarily must plead some coherent like-for-like comparative context—without turning that into a categorical, index-by-name prerequisite barred by Hughes. Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” supports screening out hindsight allegations untethered to a “sound basis for comparison,” and here the Ninth Circuit’s finding of mismatched and internally inconsistent comparisons means the complaint never plausibly connects the alleged outcomes to an imprudent process. I therefore would affirm on narrow grounds consistent with Roberts/Kagan: no per se benchmark element, but insufficient factual context on this record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry point remains the hardest issue for me because Rule 12 should not become a merits screen that denies participants any access to facts held by fiduciaries. But Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow framing—and Justice Kagan’s emphasis that ERISA’s prudence inquiry is inherently comparative—persuades me we can affirm without creating a categorical “benchmark” element: the Ninth Circuit’s “sound basis for comparison” operates here as a Rule 8 plausibility check when underperformance is offered as the proxy for imprudence, and plaintiffs remain free to plead other concrete context (fees, objectives, or process failures). Dudenhoeffer’s instruction for “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage supports requiring enough coherent context to distinguish a bad outcome from an imprudent process, and on this record the mismatched, internally inconsistent comparisons do not plausibly allege what a prudent fiduciary would have done under the circumstances then prevailing. Hughes still matters by foreclosing per se pleading rules, but it does not eliminate the need for nonconclusory factual content when the complaint’s theory is essentially “they should have done better.”

John Roberts.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is “context specific” and must be assessed with “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the Rule 12 stage, which requires nonconclusory factual allegations supporting a plausible inference that a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would have done something different under the “circumstances then prevailing.” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B); Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014). Where the theory of imprudence rests on underperformance rather than direct misconduct, some sound comparative context is ordinarily necessary to make underperformance meaningful and to avoid turning hindsight into liability—consistent with our rejection of categorical pleading rules in Hughes v. Northwestern Univ., 595 U.S. 170, 173 (2022), but still requiring plausibility under Dudenhoeffer and Iqbal. Given the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that petitioners offered generalized, internally inconsistent allegations without a “sound basis for comparison,” I would affirm on narrow grounds rather than announce a broad, categorical “benchmark” requirement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: ERISA’s text imposes a “prudent person acting in a like capacity” standard, measured against “the circumstances then prevailing,” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), which requires some objective comparator before a court may plausibly infer imprudence from mere underperformance allegations. Under this Court’s Rule 12 framework, conclusory assertions that a prudent fiduciary would have achieved better returns do not “plausibly” allege a breach; Dudenhoeffer requires “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” to separate plausible claims from meritless ones, and a meaningful benchmark supplies the necessary context. A no-benchmark rule would invite judicial second-guessing of discretionary investment judgments untethered to statutory text or historical understandings of fiduciary prudence, expanding ERISA litigation beyond its original public meaning and the limited role of federal courts. Accordingly, the Ninth Circuit’s demand for a “sound basis for comparison” is consistent with § 1104(a)(1)(B) and this Court’s pleading precedents.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is expressly tethered to “the circumstances then prevailing,” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), and this Court has required “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage to separate plausible claims from conclusory ones. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014). An underperformance theory, standing alone, is too indeterminate to plausibly imply imprudence without alleging a sound comparator—i.e., a meaningful benchmark—because absent comparative context a court cannot infer that a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would have selected materially different investments. This benchmark requirement is not a categorical merits rule forbidden by Hughes v. Northwestern Univ., 595 U.S. 170 (2022), but a practical application of Rule 8 plausibility to a context-dependent statutory standard, and it also prevents discovery-driven fishing expeditions that would unduly burden plan sponsors and fiduciaries.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence under § 404(a)(1)(B), by its terms, is “circumstances…prevailing” and “context specific,” so a categorical pleading requirement that plaintiffs must identify a particular “meaningful benchmark” risks insulating imprudent conduct at the motion-to-dismiss stage when comparative information is often uniquely in fiduciaries’ control. Under Dudenhoeffer, courts should apply “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” to separate plausible claims from conclusory ones, but that does not justify converting one evidentiary route (a benchmark) into an element of the claim. Consistent with Hughes v. Nw. Univ., bright-line pleading rules are disfavored; plaintiffs may plausibly plead imprudence through allegations of mismatched objectives, excessive fees for the strategy pursued, and persistent underperformance relative to the fund’s stated aims, with discovery and summary judgment policing merit. Requiring a benchmark as a strict prerequisite would disproportionately bar participants—often less resourced and informationally disadvantaged—from accessing judicial review of fiduciary decisionmaking under § 1104(a)(1).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: ERISA § 404(a)(1)(B) makes prudence inherently comparative and context-specific—asking what a prudent fiduciary "acting in a like capacity" would do "under the circumstances then prevailing"—so a complaint that infers imprudence solely from underperformance must supply some sound comparative context to make that inference plausible. Under Dudenhoeffer, courts must apply "careful, context-sensitive scrutiny" at the Rule 12 stage to separate plausible claims from conclusory ones, and allegations of "underperformance" without a meaningful comparator risk collapsing into the forbidden conclusory assertion that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently. This is consistent with Hughes’s rejection of rigid categorical pleading rules: plaintiffs need not plead a particular index by name in every case, but they must plead enough facts—often via an apt benchmark or peer comparison—to show like-for-like underperformance rather than merely second-guessing a different risk/strategy choice. On this record, the Ninth Circuit permissibly concluded that the complaint’s generalized attacks and mismatched comparisons did not plausibly allege imprudence under § 404(a)(1).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: ERISA’s text requires prudence to be assessed “under the circumstances then prevailing,” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), so a complaint that infers imprudence from “underperformance” must supply contextual facts that make the inference plausible rather than conclusory. Under Dudenhoeffer, courts must apply “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the Rule 12 stage to “divide the plausible sheep from the meritless goats,” and mere allegations that alternatives did better, without a sound comparator, do not plausibly show what a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would have done. Requiring some meaningful benchmark (not as a categorical pleading rule, but as a way to supply the necessary context when underperformance is the sole proxy for imprudence) follows from the statute’s comparative, circumstance-dependent standard and avoids turning ERISA into a vehicle for hindsight second-guessing. Given the complaint’s reliance on indirect underperformance allegations without a coherent basis for comparison, dismissal was proper.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: ERISA § 404(a)(1) requires prudence measured against what “a prudent man acting in a like capacity” would do under similar circumstances, and where plaintiffs infer imprudence solely from alleged underperformance or high costs, Rule 12(b)(6) plausibility demands comparative context to make that inference nonconclusory. Consistent with Dudenhoeffer’s instruction for “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleading stage, a requirement to plead a “sound basis for comparison” (a meaningful benchmark or comparator and why it is comparable) is not an atextual categorical rule but a practical application of Twombly/Iqbal-style plausibility to indirect underperformance theories. Without such a benchmark, courts risk second-guessing investment outcomes rather than policing process, inviting hindsight litigation and undermining administrable pleading standards across circuits. On this record—diversified alternative investments adopted as a post-2008 risk-mitigation strategy—the Ninth Circuit reasonably concluded the complaint did not plausibly allege imprudence absent a meaningful comparator.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is expressly “context specific,” requiring assessment of what a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would do “under the circumstances then prevailing.” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B). Under Twombly/Iqbal as applied in Fifth Third Bancorp. v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409 (2014), and reaffirmed in Hughes v. Northwestern Univ., 595 U.S. 170 (2022), a complaint must plead enough factual context to make an inference of imprudence plausible; when a claim rests on underperformance, that ordinarily requires some sound comparative context (a meaningful comparator) rather than generalized assertions or internally inconsistent narratives. Hughes rejects categorical pleading rules, but it does not relieve plaintiffs of the burden to plead facts that permit a court to infer imprudence from performance—something difficult to do without alleging a meaningful benchmark or equivalent comparative allegations. Given the statutory text’s focus on prudence “under the circumstances,” and the plausibility requirement, dismissal is appropriate where underperformance is alleged without a coherent basis for comparison.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence turns on the “circumstances … prevailing” at the time of the fiduciary’s actions, so Rule 12 review must be “careful” and “context-sensitive,” not based on conclusory inferences from bare underperformance allegations. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014), requires enough factual content to make it plausible that “a hypothetical prudent person acting in a like capacity” (29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B)) would have acted differently, and that ordinarily demands some comparative context—i.e., a sound basis for comparison—rather than generalized attacks on asset classes or hindsight second-guessing. While Hughes v. Northwestern Univ., 595 U.S. 170, 173 (2022), cautions against categorical pleading rules, requiring a meaningful comparator here functions as a practical plausibility check tied to context, not a rigid per se rule. Given the complaint’s internally inconsistent theory and lack of a plausible benchmark to separate prudent risk-mitigation choices from imprudence, dismissal was appropriate at the pleading stage.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ERISA plaintiffs alleging fiduciary imprudence based on investment underperformance must plead a ‘meaningful benchmark’ to plausibly state a claim under the federal pleading standard.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA § 404(a)(1), 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) (duty of prudence and related fiduciary duties); implicitly Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 8(a) as interpreted by Twombly/Iqbal (pleading plausibility); tangentially Article III standing principles (for the separate document-request/‘informational injury’ discussion).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners contend that a claim alleging underperformance and imprudent investment decisionmaking should not be dismissed merely for failure to plead a particular ‘meaningful benchmark’; alleging that fiduciaries failed to act with ERISA-required ‘care, skill, prudence, or diligence’ in light of underperformance should suffice at the pleading stage without needing a specific comparator index/peer group/alternative investment that is sufficiently similar in risk, strategy, and composition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that underperformance alone is not enough to plausibly plead imprudence because ERISA prudence is process- and context-dependent; plaintiffs must allege a sound basis for comparison (a meaningful benchmark) to support the inference that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently under similar circumstances—especially where the Plans pursued an atypical post-2008 risk-mitigation strategy using diversified portfolios including alternatives (hedge funds/private equity). They also argue the case is a poor vehicle (fact-bound, atypical strategy/allocations, and other issues), and that plaintiffs’ generalized critiques of alternative investments fail to connect to the actual holdings and portfolio-level objectives. Separately, on the ERISA document-request claim/standing discussion in the record, respondents rely on Supreme Court standing doctrine to argue that a bare statutory/procedural violation or omitted information, without concrete harm, does not establish Article III injury-in-fact.

Va. Military Institute v. United States, 508 U.S. 946 (1993)
Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 541 U.S. 913 (2004)
Thole v. U.S. Bank N.A., 140 S. Ct. 1615 (2020)
Magadia v. Wal-Mart Associates, Inc., 999 F.3d 668 (9th Cir. 2021)
Strubel v. Comenity Bank, 842 F.3d 181 (2d Cir. 2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that Hughes warns against categorical, atextual pleading hurdles, and I agree we should not announce any across-the-board “meaningful benchmark” prerequisite. But Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh correctly tie Rule 8 plausibility to ERISA’s text—prudence “under the circumstances then prevailing” and “like capacity”—which means an underperformance theory about an atypical strategy needs some nonconclusory contextual anchor making it plausible a prudent fiduciary with like aims would have acted differently; otherwise, as Justice Alito notes, the complaint is essentially hindsight and apples-to-oranges. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern is real, yet Twombly/Iqbal do not relax plausibility because process facts are in defendants’ hands, and without a like-for-like comparator or equivalent context here, the inference of imprudence remains speculative. A narrow affirmance—case-specific, disavowing any universal benchmark element—best respects Hughes while applying Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the pleadings stage.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Hughes rejects categorical, atextual pleading hurdles, so we should not announce a universal “meaningful benchmark” element. But that does not relieve plaintiffs of Rule 8’s plausibility requirement as applied to ERISA’s text: § 1104(a)(1)(B) ties prudence to “the circumstances then prevailing,” so an underperformance theory must plead contextual facts making it plausible that a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would have made a different choice, rather than merely alleging lagging returns with hindsight. Chief Justice Roberts’ narrower framing answers Hughes’s concern: we can affirm on the ground that, given an atypical strategy, the complaint offers no meaningful like-for-like reference point (or equivalent contextual allegations) and thus remains conclusory and apples-to-oranges, without converting comparators into a rigid prerequisite. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry argument is ultimately a policy plea that cannot override Twombly/Iqbal’s demand for nonconclusory factual content at the outset.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that we must not let “meaningful benchmark” harden into a categorical pleading prerequisite contrary to Hughes, but that concern is answered if we frame the inquiry as ordinary Twombly/Iqbal plausibility applied to ERISA’s text requiring prudence “under the circumstances then prevailing.” As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, when plaintiffs’ theory is sustained underperformance of an atypical, risk-mitigating strategy, the complaint must plead some nonconclusory context—often a like-for-like comparator or equivalent facts—showing that a prudent fiduciary with like aims would have acted differently; otherwise the inference of imprudence is speculative and invites hindsight. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry objection is a real policy concern, but it cannot dilute Rule 8 plausibility where the complaint’s own theory depends on relative performance without facts tying the lag to imprudence rather than a chosen risk/return tradeoff. Properly read, Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” permits dismissal here without announcing any across-the-board benchmark element, and thus does not conflict with Hughes’s rejection of categorical safe harbors.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point that, for an atypical strategy, Twombly/Iqbal plus Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” requires some nonconclusory anchor showing a prudent fiduciary with like aims might have acted differently, and I agree courts should reject pure apples-to-oranges underperformance claims. But I cannot accept their practical move—treating a like-for-like comparator as effectively outcome-determinative here—because Hughes warns against categorical pleading gates, and § 1104(a)(1)(B) asks about prudence under the circumstances, which can be plausibly alleged through other concrete indicia of a flawed process (e.g., persistent excessive fees, failure to monitor, and available cheaper alternatives) even without an internal “perfect match” benchmark. Justice Thomas is right that “circumstances then prevailing” matters, yet that cuts both ways: information asymmetry about fiduciaries’ monitoring and negotiations makes it inappropriate to demand the very comparator/process details uniquely held by defendants at Rule 12 when plaintiffs plead specific external facts suggesting mismanagement. Under my pragmatic approach attentive to access to justice, we should reverse and require a truly context-sensitive plausibility analysis that permits claims to proceed when the pleaded facts plausibly indicate an imprudent process, not just a missing benchmark.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point: Dudenhoeffer requires “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at Rule 12, and Twombly/Iqbal demand some nonconclusory factual anchor that a prudent fiduciary with like aims would have acted differently—especially to avoid apples-to-oranges hindsight in atypical-strategy underperformance claims. But their proposed affirmance still risks making the absence of a like-for-like “meaningful benchmark” outcome-determinative in practice, which effectively hardens into the categorical pleading gate Hughes cautioned against, because § 1104(a)(1)(B) asks about prudence “under the circumstances then prevailing,” not about a particular comparator form. I agree comparators will often be the clearest way to plead context, yet I would reverse to clarify that courts must evaluate all pleaded, specific contextual facts (fees, stated strategy, duration, available alternatives, monitoring allegations) to decide plausibility case-by-case rather than treating a benchmark’s absence as dispositive. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on comparators as the ‘most direct’ context is persuasive as a generality, but not enough to justify a rule that functionally screens out potentially plausible process-based imprudence claims at the threshold.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point that Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny,” filtered through Twombly/Iqbal and ERISA’s “circumstances then prevailing,” requires some concrete, nonconclusory basis to infer that a prudent fiduciary with like aims would have acted differently—often supplied by a comparator. But even framed as “not categorical,” their approach risks making the absence of a like-for-like benchmark dispositive in underperformance cases, which functionally adds an atextual pleading element and runs headlong into Hughes’s warning against gatekeeping rules that short-circuit § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s circumstance-specific inquiry. Justice Thomas is right that context is essential to avoid apples-to-oranges hindsight, yet that contextual showing can come from other pleaded facts (fees, stated strategy, duration, plausible alternatives, monitoring failures) and should be assessed case-by-case rather than by elevating one evidentiary tool into a practical prerequisite. Policy concerns about discovery costs, emphasized by Justice Alito, are real but cannot justify reworking Rule 8 or ERISA’s text; ordinary plausibility review already empowers dismissal of conclusory complaints.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that Hughes warns against categorical, atextual pleading hurdles, and I agree we should not constitutionalize (or ERISA-ize) a universal “meaningful benchmark” element. But as the Chief Justice explains, Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny,” applied through Twombly/Iqbal and ERISA’s “circumstances then prevailing,” still requires some concrete, nonconclusory context making it plausible that a prudent fiduciary with like aims would have acted differently; for an atypical, risk-mitigating strategy, a like-for-like comparator (or its functional equivalent) is ordinarily the only practical way to supply that context and avoid hindsight/apples-to-oranges pleading. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern is real, but it cannot relax Rule 8 plausibility where the theory of imprudence turns on relative performance and fees without facts tying those outcomes to an imprudent decision under the plan’s chosen strategy. On these allegations, dismissal can be affirmed narrowly—without announcing a rigid benchmark prerequisite for all ERISA imprudence complaints.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point for affirmance: in an underperformance case involving an atypical strategy, a like-for-like comparator is often the most reliable way to supply the “circumstances then prevailing” context and avoid hindsight under Twombly/Iqbal and Dudenhoeffer. But under a textualist reading of § 1104(a)(1)(B), that practical evidentiary point cannot be converted into a dispositive pleading gate, because the statute asks about prudence “under the circumstances,” not about the presence of a particular benchmark allegation. Hughes reinforces that we should not harden one useful pleading tool into a categorical rule; courts can still dismiss apples-to-oranges or conclusory complaints for lack of contextual facts without treating a near-identical comparator as outcome-determinative. Justice Thomas is right that comparators are an “ordinary means” of supplying context, yet in this case the respondent-side approach risks functioning as an extra-textual prerequisite rather than a case-by-case plausibility assessment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point that, for an atypical strategy, a like-for-like comparator is often the clearest way to supply the “circumstances then prevailing” context and to avoid hindsight pleading under Dudenhoeffer and Twombly/Iqbal. But even taking that seriously, I do not think the absence of a near-identical benchmark can do dispositive work at Rule 12 without effectively hardening into the categorical gatekeeping Hughes warns against, because § 1104(a)(1)(B) asks about prudence in context, not a particular pleading form. Justice Thomas is right that plaintiffs must allege nonconclusory facts making it plausible a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would have acted differently, yet that plausibility can sometimes be supplied by other concrete allegations (fees, monitoring failures, duration, and strategy drift) that—considered together—permit a reasonable inference of an imprudent process despite information asymmetry. Under my pragmatic, procedural-fairness approach, we should reverse to require a genuinely case-by-case plausibility analysis, treating benchmarks as helpful evidence, not as an effectively mandatory prerequisite in this subset of cases.

John Roberts.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is expressly “context specific,” requiring inquiry into “the circumstances … prevailing” when the fiduciary acted, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), and our cases require “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the Rule 12 stage to separate plausible from conclusory claims. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014). Where plaintiffs infer imprudence solely from underperformance (and fees) rather than alleging concrete process failures, Twombly/Iqbal plausibility demands allegations permitting a reasonable inference that a prudent fiduciary “with like aims” would have acted differently—typically requiring a sound comparator or “meaningful benchmark” rather than an apples-to-oranges comparison. That approach is consistent with rejecting categorical rules (Hughes v. Nw.
